title: Aspen Dental Twilio Demo: Panel Rebuttal Prep
subtitle: 60 likely questions from the October 7 panel, with five-sentence answers
author: Brian Athey
how_to_use: Each answer follows the same five beats: acknowledge, answer directly, give the evidence, name the trade-off honestly, then tie back to the asker's goal or check in.
Say the first two sentences even if you are short on time; they carry the answer.
Where a number depends on pricing, contract terms, or carrier rules, the answer commits to confirming it rather than guessing.
Personas are fictional, created for the exercise; company facts come from the Aspen Dental account brief.

personas.name: Luyba Caloras
personas.lens: Revenue, no-show rate, consistency across offices, risk, and what she has to decide.

questions.q: What return should we expect, and how quickly?
questions.a: That's the right first question, because the business case has to stand on its own. Each 1-point drop in no-shows recovers roughly 6,000 visits a month across the network, which is about $11M to $22M a year at $150 to $300 per visit. Commure saw 54% fewer no-shows for preventive screenings with a similar multichannel approach, so a 2-point target is conservative. The honest caveat is that those dollar figures are illustrative until we baseline your real no-show rate in the pilot offices. A 30-day, two-office pilot gives you a measured number before you commit to a network rollout.

questions.q: How confident are you in the $11M to $22M figure?
questions.a: I'd call it directionally sound, not audited. It starts from Aspen's own published figure of more than 30,000 patients a day, takes 1% of those visits, and applies a $150 to $300 value per visit. The math is simple on purpose so your finance team can swap in real visit values in a few minutes. Where it could be wrong is the per-visit value and the baseline no-show rate, which vary by office and procedure mix. That is exactly why the first decision on the table is a pilot that replaces my assumptions with your data.

questions.q: Why Twilio instead of the reminder feature in our practice-management system?
questions.a: Built-in reminders are a reasonable starting point, and many offices probably use them today. The gap is that they usually support one or two channels, offer limited control over fallback logic, and vary by system, which works against one consistent Aspen voice. Twilio gives you SMS, voice, WhatsApp, and email on one platform, with Lookup to pick the right channel per patient and status callbacks to prove what was delivered. The trade-off is that you own an integration rather than flipping a switch. For a 1,100-office network that wants consistency and measurable outcomes, that control is the point.

questions.q: What will this cost us?
questions.a: I'll give you the structure now and have the account executive bring exact pricing, since it depends on volume and contract terms. Twilio is usage-based, so you pay per message, per call minute, per lookup, and per email, with volume discounts at your scale. There are also one-time and recurring A2P registration fees, plus carrier pass-through fees on SMS. Against the opportunity, even a generous messaging budget is a small fraction of one recovered visit per office per day. I'd suggest we size the pilot cost together so you see a real number next to the measured no-show change.

questions.q: How long until a pilot is live?
questions.a: Realistically four to six weeks, and the long pole isn't the code. The integration and reminder logic can be built in parallel in a couple of weeks, since you've just seen a working version. A2P brand and campaign registration is the critical path, because carriers must approve the campaign before SMS delivers. Voice, email, and WhatsApp can start sooner, so the pilot doesn't have to wait on SMS to begin measuring. Starting registration this week is the single biggest lever on the timeline.

questions.q: What does the pilot need from my team?
questions.a: Less than most projects, but a few things only Aspen can provide. We need two pilot offices, a named owner on your side, access to appointment data from the scheduling system, and your current opt-in language. Legal needs to confirm which entity registers the A2P brand and sign the BAA. Front-desk staff need about an hour of orientation on the new staff queue. In return, you get a weekly readout on confirm rate, no-show rate, and staff time saved.

questions.q: How do we keep one brand when every practice is independently owned?
questions.a: That's the structural question that makes Aspen different from a single-owner group. The cleanest model is one Standard brand registered under the entity that runs patient communications, with every practice sending through one Messaging Service. Patients then see consistent Aspen Dental messaging from local clinic numbers, which builds trust. The open question is legal, not technical: whether ADMI, TAG, or each practice should own the registration. I'd want your legal team's view before we lock that in, because it affects the EIN on the brand.

questions.q: Who should own the A2P registration: ADMI, TAG, or each practice?
questions.a: My recommendation is ADMI, assuming it already provides patient communications as a shared service. One brand under one EIN keeps registration, compliance, and throughput in one place, instead of a thousand separate filings. Per-practice registration is possible but multiplies the paperwork and fragments your sender reputation. TAG-level registration could make sense if you plan to extend this to ClearChoice or WellNow. I'd frame it as a 15-minute decision with legal once we confirm who signs patient-communication agreements today.

questions.q: What if patients find reminders annoying and opt out?
questions.a: Opt-outs are a real risk, and the design should earn the patient's attention rather than spend it. The patient journey caps reminders at three touches, stops the moment the patient answers, and uses each patient's preferred channel first. STOP and HELP are handled automatically by the Messaging Service, so an opt-out is honored instantly and logged. We'd track opt-out rate in the pilot right next to confirm rate. If opt-outs climb, we change cadence or wording before scaling, which is exactly what a pilot is for.

questions.q: How does this scale to 1,100 offices?
questions.a: The platform side scales well; the operational side is where planning matters. Twilio already handles very large messaging volumes, and a Messaging Service spreads traffic across a pool of sender numbers. Throughput is tied to your campaign's trust score, which is why a Standard brand with secondary vetting matters. The real scaling work is office onboarding, number provisioning, and front-desk training, which we'd sequence in waves after the pilot. I'd propose a wave plan by region once the pilot proves the result.

questions.q: What is the risk if carriers block our messages?
questions.a: It's the most important compliance risk, and I'm living it in this demo. Unregistered SMS is blocked with error 30034, which is why my SMS is simulated today. Proper registration, clear opt-in, and content that matches the approved campaign are what keep messages flowing. Even with registration, carriers can filter content that looks like spam, so we monitor delivery status, not just sends. Having voice, email, and WhatsApp in the mix means a carrier issue never leaves a patient unreached.

questions.q: Can we refill cancelled appointments?
questions.a: Yes, and that's where reminders turn into revenue rather than just fewer empty chairs. When a patient cancels, the system can release the slot back to the schedule and notify patients on a waitlist. The same Twilio channels send the offer, and the first patient to accept gets the slot. The trade-off is that waitlist logic lives in your scheduling system or our integration layer, so it's a phase-two feature. I'd include it in the pilot design so we can measure refills, not just confirmations.

questions.q: How do we measure success and report it to the board?
questions.a: With three numbers you already care about, measured against a baseline. Confirm rate, no-show rate, and front-desk hours saved, compared between pilot offices and similar control offices. Twilio's delivery data and the reply outcomes give us an audit trail for every reminder. We'd convert recovered visits to dollars using your own per-visit values, so finance trusts the number. I'd suggest a one-page weekly readout during the pilot and a board-ready summary at day 30.

questions.q: Why not just hire more front-desk staff?
questions.a: Staffing is a valid option, and some offices may need it regardless. The problem is that calling patients doesn't scale: at roughly two hours a day per office, that's a large hidden cost across 1,100 offices. Automated reminders handle the routine confirmations so staff focus on the exceptions and the patients in front of them. This isn't about replacing people; it's about moving them to work that needs a human. Most groups find staff are relieved to stop making confirmation calls.

questions.q: What advantage does this give us over other dental groups?
questions.a: Patient experience is becoming a competitive differentiator, especially for access-focused brands like Aspen. Reaching patients on the channel they actually use, including WhatsApp for a growing Hispanic patient base, is a visible upgrade. Consistency across 1,100 offices is hard for smaller groups to match. Operationally, better show rates mean more revenue from the same chairs and staff. I'd be careful not to overclaim, though: the advantage comes from executing well, not from the technology alone.

questions.q: What's the biggest risk to this project?
questions.a: Honestly, it's registration and data access, not the Twilio APIs. If A2P approval is slow, SMS waits, which is why we start registration in week one and run other channels in parallel. If appointment data is hard to extract from the scheduling system, integration takes longer. Change management at the front desk is the third risk, which we address with a simple staff queue and training. None of these are blockers, but each needs an owner on day one.

questions.q: Could this extend to ClearChoice and the other TAG brands?
questions.a: Yes, and that's a strong reason to design it once and well. The same reminder pattern applies to implant consultations, urgent care follow-ups, and other appointment-driven businesses. If TAG becomes the registering entity, separate campaigns can cover each brand's use case under one governance model. I'd keep the pilot focused on Aspen Dental so we don't dilute the result. Once it's proven, the expansion case largely writes itself.

questions.q: What does Twilio commit to on reliability and support?
questions.a: That's a fair contract question, and I'd rather give you the exact terms than paraphrase them. Twilio publishes service-level commitments and offers paid support tiers with defined response times for enterprise customers. The architecture also protects you: fallback URLs, status callbacks, and multiple channels mean a single failure doesn't stop reminders. The account executive will bring the specific SLA and support options that fit Aspen's scale. I'd recommend reviewing them alongside the BAA so legal sees everything at once.

questions.q: Should we wait for AI voice agents instead?
questions.a: No, but you should design so AI can plug in later. The reminder-and-confirm workflow delivers value now and gives you the data an AI agent would need anyway. Twilio's ConversationRelay lets an AI voice agent handle the reschedule conversation, which is what Docplanner did to double bookings at lower cost. A sensible path is to launch structured reminders first, then add an AI agent for reschedules in phase two. That way you bank results now and avoid betting the pilot on a newer technology.

questions.q: If I could decide one thing today, what should it be?
questions.a: Approve the two-office pilot with a 2-point no-show target. Everything else follows from that decision: registration, the BAA, and office selection all become concrete tasks with owners. It's low risk, because the pilot is small, time-boxed, and measured against a baseline. It also answers your question about results with your data instead of my estimates. Can we agree on the pilot today and confirm the two offices with Zach this week?

personas.name: Dustin Berg
personas.lens: Integration, security, HIPAA, failure modes, and whether the build is production-grade.

questions.q: How does this integrate with our scheduling or EHR system?
questions.a: The integration point is appointment data in and outcomes out, nothing more invasive. A small reminder service reads upcoming appointments through your system's API, an HL7 or FHIR interface, or a scheduled export, depending on what you expose. It calls Twilio's REST APIs to send reminders and receives replies and status callbacks on signed webhooks. Outcomes such as confirmed, cancelled, or reschedule requested write back to the schedule. I'd want to understand your system's interfaces first, since that drives the integration estimate more than Twilio does.

questions.q: Walk me through what happens when a webhook fails.
questions.a: Failure handling was a design goal, not an afterthought. If my server is unreachable when Twilio fetches voice instructions, the caller hears Twilio's application error, which you saw is a real risk with a demo tunnel. In production, each number gets a fallback URL so Twilio retries a secondary endpoint, and the service runs on hosted, monitored infrastructure. Status callbacks are processed idempotently, so a retry doesn't double-count an outcome. I'd also set alerts on webhook errors so we know before patients do.

questions.q: How do you validate that webhooks really come from Twilio?
questions.a: Every Twilio webhook carries an X-Twilio-Signature header, which is an HMAC of the full URL and posted parameters. My app recomputes that signature with the account's Auth Token and rejects anything that doesn't match. The URL has to match exactly, scheme, host, and path, which is a common gotcha behind proxies and tunnels. Validation happens before any business logic runs. Email replies through SendGrid Inbound Parse don't carry that signature, so that endpoint needs separate protection.

questions.q: Why doesn't a 201 response mean the message was delivered?
questions.a: Because the REST call and the delivery are two separate events. A 201 Created means Twilio accepted the request and queued the message or call, nothing more. Delivery is reported later through status callbacks, moving through statuses like sent, delivered, or failed for messages, and initiated through completed for calls. My dashboard treats queued as pending until a callback confirms the outcome. In production, reporting delivered on a 201 would overstate your confirm rate, so we only count confirmed callbacks.

questions.q: How do you handle duplicate or out-of-order status callbacks?
questions.a: You should assume both will happen, because callbacks are delivered over the internet with retries. Each callback carries the message or call SID and its status, so I key updates on the SID. Statuses are ranked, so a late sent callback can never overwrite a delivered one. Writes are idempotent, which makes duplicate callbacks harmless. That logic is small but important, since it's what keeps reporting accurate.

questions.q: Is this HIPAA compliant, and what do we need to do?
questions.a: HIPAA compliance is shared, so I'd describe it as HIPAA-ready rather than compliant out of the box. Twilio signs a Business Associate Agreement for its HIPAA-eligible products on qualifying plans, and that BAA has to be in place before any PHI flows. On Aspen's side, we keep message content minimum-necessary, keep PHI out of logs, and restrict access to the reminder service. My demo uses no real patient data, which is the correct posture before a BAA. I'd ask legal to review the BAA and the eligible-product list as part of the pilot decision.

questions.q: How do you keep PHI out of messages and logs?
questions.a: The simplest rule is that reminders don't need clinical details to work. A message says you have an appointment Friday at 10 AM at your local office, with no procedure, provider specialty, or diagnosis. Application logs record SIDs, statuses, and outcomes, not message bodies or patient names. Twilio's own message logs should also be configured with that in mind, so content stays minimal there too. We'd review the templates with your compliance team before launch.

questions.q: Email replies are unsigned. How would you secure that endpoint?
questions.a: You caught a real gap, and I call it out on the architecture slide. SendGrid Inbound Parse posts raw email to my endpoint without a Twilio-style signature. In production, I'd protect it with HTTP basic auth in the parse URL, a hard-to-guess path, and validation that the recipient address and message format match what we sent. I'd also rate-limit the endpoint and treat every reply as untrusted input. The reply only updates an appointment state, so even a forged reply can't expose data.

questions.q: How do you manage credentials?
questions.a: I separate REST credentials from webhook validation. REST calls use an API key and secret scoped to the service, so keys can be rotated or revoked without touching the main account. The Auth Token is used only to validate incoming webhook signatures. All secrets live in environment variables, never in code, and in production they'd sit in a secrets manager. I'd also use subaccounts to isolate development, staging, and production.

questions.q: Can we send a whole day's reminders at once?
questions.a: Yes, but throughput is set by registration, not just by code. A Messaging Service queues outbound messages and sends at the rate your campaign is approved for. A Standard brand with secondary vetting gets a higher trust score, which raises throughput and daily caps. If a burst exceeds the rate, messages queue rather than fail. I'd still spread sends across the morning to stay within quiet hours and avoid carrier filtering.

questions.q: How does Lookup routing work, and is it worth the cost?
questions.a: Lookup v2 line type intelligence tells us whether a number is mobile, landline, or VoIP before we send. That lets us skip SMS for landlines and go straight to voice, which avoids failed sends. Lookup is billed per request, so I'd cache results and re-check periodically instead of on every reminder. The account executive can confirm per-lookup pricing at your volume. Given the cost of a missed patient, a cached lookup per number usually pays for itself quickly.

questions.q: What happens with landlines that can't receive texts?
questions.a: They get a voice call instead, which is the point of routing. Lookup flags the number as a landline, and the service skips SMS and WhatsApp for that patient. The call reads the appointment details and asks them to press 1 to confirm or 2 to reschedule. If no one answers, answering-machine detection can leave a short message. That's how Zachary's requirement to reach every patient is met technically.

questions.q: How is consent stored, and does an opt-out apply across channels?
questions.a: Consent should live in Aspen's system of record, with Twilio enforcing it at the edge. The Messaging Service automatically handles STOP and HELP keywords for SMS and records the opt-out. Our service listens for those events and marks the patient opted out across all channels, not just the one they used. Consent captured at intake is stored with a timestamp and source, which is also the evidence carriers expect for campaign approval. I'd verify that cross-channel rule with your compliance team, since some practices may treat channels differently.

questions.q: What about answering machines on voice calls?
questions.a: Twilio's answering-machine detection can tell a human from voicemail when the call is answered. When a machine is detected, the call plays a one-shot message without the keypad prompt. I built that path, but left it off for the live demo because detection adds a short delay and a small cost. In production, I'd turn it on and tune it in the pilot. I'd also keep the voicemail script short and free of PHI.

questions.q: Why a tunnel, and how would this be hosted in production?
questions.a: The tunnel exists only because my demo runs on a laptop. Twilio needs a public HTTPS URL to fetch voice instructions and post callbacks, and a Cloudflare tunnel provides that temporarily. In production, the service runs in Aspen's cloud environment behind a stable domain, TLS, and a load balancer. Fallback URLs point to a secondary region for resilience. The tunnel is a demo convenience, not part of the recommended architecture.

questions.q: How do we test without messaging real patients?
questions.a: Separate environments and test data are non-negotiable here. Subaccounts isolate development and staging from production, each with its own numbers and credentials. Twilio provides test credentials for exercising API calls without sending real traffic. For end-to-end tests, we'd use staff phones and inboxes, the way I'm demoing with my own Gmail, WhatsApp, and AT&T line. Production patient data only enters after the BAA and a staged rollout.

questions.q: What's the monitoring and observability story?
questions.a: I'd monitor at three levels: Twilio, the application, and the business outcome. Twilio's Console debugger and error alerts surface failed webhooks and delivery errors, and Event Streams can push message and call events into your data platform. The application tracks webhook latency, validation failures, and queue depth. The business dashboard shows confirm rate and no-show rate by office. Alerts go to engineering on errors and to operations on outcome drops.

questions.q: How do you handle time zones and quiet hours?
questions.a: Every send is scheduled in the office's local time zone, not the server's. Each office record carries its time zone, and the scheduler only sends inside an allowed window, such as 8 AM to 8 PM local time. Reminders that would fall outside the window shift to the next allowed slot. That matters for patient experience and for compliance with rules on messaging times. Across 47 states, I'd treat this as a required feature, not a nice-to-have.

questions.q: Did AI write this code, and how do you know it's correct?
questions.a: I used Claude and OpenAI as coding assistants in Cursor, and I'm comfortable saying so. The design decisions, such as webhook validation, idempotent callbacks, and the fallback path, are mine. More importantly, I checked every Twilio endpoint against Twilio's published OpenAPI specs instead of trusting generated code. I also tested each channel end to end, which is how I found real issues like the tunnel URL changing on restart. AI made me faster; verification is what makes it trustworthy.

questions.q: What would you change before this goes to production?
questions.a: Quite a bit, and I'd rather name it than have you find it. The tunnel becomes hosted HTTPS with fallback URLs, and SQLite becomes write-back to the scheduling system. The WhatsApp sandbox becomes a registered business sender, and SMS moves to a Standard brand on an approved campaign. I'd add the email endpoint protections, secrets management, monitoring, and quiet-hour scheduling. None of that changes the core pattern you saw, but all of it is required before patient data flows.

personas.name: Zachary Treiber
personas.lens: The patient's experience, front-desk workload, adoption, and practical next steps. In real life a Twilio sales director, so expect deal-progression questions too.

questions.q: How do we reach patients who ignore texts?
questions.a: By not depending on texts alone. The journey starts with the patient's preferred channel and escalates if there's no response: email, then SMS or WhatsApp, then a voice call. Lookup tells us which channels a number can actually receive. If a patient still hasn't answered 12 hours out, the appointment goes to the front desk for a personal call. That way, every patient gets a path that fits how they communicate.

questions.q: What does the patient actually see or hear?
questions.a: Something short, branded, and easy to act on. A text or WhatsApp message names Aspen Dental, the office, and the time, and asks for a one-letter reply. The email asks for a one-word reply, and the voice call asks them to press 1 to confirm or 2 to reschedule. You saw each of those live in the demo. We'd refine the wording with your team and test it in the pilot.

questions.q: How does a reschedule request get to a person?
questions.a: A reschedule reply never hits a dead end. When a patient presses 2 or replies R or reschedule, the system flags the appointment and places it in a staff queue. The front desk sees who needs a call and why, ordered by appointment time. In a fuller build, TaskRouter can route those tasks to the right office or a central team. Later, an AI voice agent could handle simple reschedules and pass harder ones to staff.

questions.q: Why include WhatsApp?
questions.a: Because a growing share of your Hispanic patients told you they prefer it. Your recent patient survey made WhatsApp a new engagement channel, not just a fallback. WhatsApp messages are free to receive over data, familiar, and widely used in many Latin American communities. Business-initiated messages use pre-approved templates, which keeps them consistent and compliant. I'd let patients opt into WhatsApp at intake and measure its confirm rate against SMS in the pilot.

questions.q: Can reminders go out in Spanish?
questions.a: Yes, and for Aspen's patient base I'd treat it as essential. Message and email templates can be written in Spanish, and WhatsApp templates are approved per language. Voice calls can use Spanish text-to-speech voices, so the call sounds natural rather than translated. The patient's language preference would come from intake, just like their channel preference. I'd have native speakers review the wording before launch.

questions.q: How many reminders is too many?
questions.a: More than three starts to feel like nagging. The journey I showed uses up to three automated touches: 72 hours, 48 hours, and 24 hours out. Every reminder stops the moment the patient responds, so most patients get one or two. We'd watch opt-out rates by office during the pilot. If opt-outs rise, we cut a touch or change timing before scaling.

questions.q: What happens if a patient replies with something unexpected?
questions.a: The system shouldn't guess, and it shouldn't ignore them. Clear replies like C, R, confirm, or cancel are handled automatically. Anything else, such as a question about insurance, goes to the staff queue so a person can answer. We can also reply with a short message that lists the valid options. Over time, the unexpected replies tell us what patients actually want, which shapes the next version.

questions.q: How does the front desk see what's happening?
questions.a: Through a simple view of today's and tomorrow's appointments with a status for each. Confirmed, rescheduling, no response, and opted out are shown at a glance, like the dashboard in my demo. The staff queue lists only the patients who need a human. In production, that status would ideally appear inside the scheduling system they already use. The goal is fewer screens for staff, not one more.

questions.q: How should we pick the two pilot offices?
questions.a: Pick offices that will give a clean, credible result. I'd choose two offices with above-average no-show rates, a reasonable mix of patients, and office managers who want to try something new. Matching each with a similar control office lets us compare fairly. One office with a strong Hispanic patient base would let us test WhatsApp properly. You know your offices far better than I do, so I'd want your shortlist.

questions.q: What training does the front desk need?
questions.a: About an hour, because the system removes work rather than adding it. Staff learn to read the status view, work the staff queue, and handle opt-out questions. We'd give them a one-page guide and a contact for issues during the pilot. Their feedback in the first two weeks would shape changes before scaling. If training takes much longer than an hour, the design is too complicated.

questions.q: Can patients choose their channel?
questions.a: Yes, and they should. At intake, patients can choose text, WhatsApp, email, or phone, and their language. Lookup fills in the gaps, for example by routing a landline to voice automatically. Patients can change their preference at any time, and an opt-out on one channel is respected across all of them. Choice is what makes reminders feel like service instead of spam.

questions.q: What about elderly patients or patients with accessibility needs?
questions.a: Voice is often the best channel for them, and it's built in. Many older patients still rely on landlines, which Lookup detects and routes to a call. The call uses clear speech, repeats the prompt, and accepts a simple keypress. Patients can also designate a caregiver's number if that's their preference. We'd test the call script with real patients in the pilot to make sure it's easy to follow.

questions.q: What if a patient's phone number is wrong?
questions.a: Then the system tells us, which is better than silence. Lookup and delivery status reveal invalid, disconnected, or unreachable numbers. Those appointments go straight to the staff queue, along with a note to update the patient's contact details. Email acts as a backup channel when the phone fails. Over the pilot, this also cleans up your contact data, which benefits every future reminder.

questions.q: Will this replace front-desk jobs?
questions.a: No, and I'd be careful to position it that way with staff. It replaces the repetitive confirmation calls, roughly two hours a day per office in our assumptions. Those hours go back to patients in the office, insurance questions, and the reschedules that need a person. Staff become the escalation path for the patients who need them most. In most practices, that makes the job better, not smaller.

questions.q: Can patients reschedule themselves with a link?
questions.a: Yes, as a natural next step. A reminder can include a short link to the scheduling page, ideally on an Aspen-branded domain so patients trust it. The link must be declared in the A2P campaign, because undeclared links can trigger carrier filtering. I'd keep the link free of patient details and require the patient to identify themselves on the page. It's a good phase-two feature once the core reminders prove out.

questions.q: How do we collect consent at intake without slowing check-in?
questions.a: Make it one question on a form patients already fill out. A single checkbox asking how they'd like reminders, with a clear statement of what they'll receive and how to stop, covers it. The response is stored with a timestamp, which is also the evidence carriers require for campaign approval. Digital intake forms make this effortless; paper forms just need the same wording. Your team would review the language with legal before the pilot.

questions.q: How long does it take to get a production WhatsApp sender?
questions.a: Longer than the sandbox, so we'd start early. Today I'm using Twilio's WhatsApp sandbox, which is meant for testing. Production requires a WhatsApp Business sender tied to Aspen's verified Meta business, an approved display name, and approved message templates. Approval timelines vary, so I'd start that process alongside A2P registration in week one. The pilot can launch on voice and email while WhatsApp approval completes.

questions.q: Could we also send post-visit follow-ups or review requests?
questions.a: Yes, the same platform supports the full patient journey. Post-visit messages, treatment follow-ups, and recall reminders use the same channels and consent model. Each use case may need its own A2P campaign, especially anything that looks like marketing. I'd keep the pilot focused on appointment reminders so the result is clean. Once that's proven, follow-ups and recall are logical next steps.

questions.q: What's the next step, and who needs to be in the room?
questions.a: The next step is a pilot kickoff within two weeks. Luyba approves the pilot and the target, legal decides the registering entity and reviews the BAA, Dustin names an engineering owner, and you pick the two offices. On our side, the account executive brings pricing and contract terms, and I lead the technical design. We'd leave the kickoff with registration started and a 30-day plan. Can we put that meeting on the calendar before we wrap today?

questions.q: What did you learn building this that would help us?
questions.a: Three lessons, and all of them apply to Aspen. First, registration is the long pole, which I learned firsthand when my SMS was blocked during carrier review. Second, small details like an exact webhook URL or a time zone decide whether a system is reliable, so they need to be designed, not discovered. Third, multiple channels aren't a luxury; they're how you keep reaching patients when one channel fails. Those lessons are built into the plan I'm recommending.
